questions.question: What motivated you to go on exchange? (pick the most important one) *
questions.answer: Academic opportunities

questions.question: Which aspects were crucial to choosing your study destination? *
questions.answer: I wanted to go to a university with a high level of teaching, and the University of Bergen has a good reputation especially for its high quality courses in Nordic literature. Furthermore, I wanted to broaden my knowledge and academic skills, so I took the opportunity to take a course in ethnomusicology, because I have always been interested in the topic. Lastly, it was important for me to go somewhere with beautiful nature, because there is not much of that in Denmark and the mountains in the Bergen area are gorgeous!

questions.question: How would you rate your overall study abroad experience? *
Additional comments:
questions.answer: It was a fantastic experience to study abroad, but it was also tough at times. It takes time to get used to the new place and the courses you will be taking.

questions.question: How easy was it to find the information you needed to know upon arrival? *
questions.answer: It was quite easy if you keep attention to the information you get before your arrival, and the information you get through UiB's own e-mails and digital systems.

questions.question: What assistance, if any, did you receive when you arrived at your study destination? *
questions.answer: There was an orientation day for international students and an orientation day at the faculty I attended to. Besides that, the study guide was very helpful with information. However, it sometimes took them a bit long time to respond over e-mail.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the orientation and assistance available to students at your host institution upon arrival? *
Additional comments
How did you find housing? *
questions.answer: I found housing through my host institution

questions.question: Did you live on campus or off campus? *
questions.answer: Off campus

questions.question: How easy was it to find off campus housing? Any recommendations? *
questions.answer: I was automatically given a dorm room through the student association SAMMEN, when I was accepted as an international student at UiB.

questions.question: What should future exchange students know about living off campus? *
questions.answer: I lived in a dormitory with a shared kitchen with 9 other people but with my own room and bathroom. Here I met most of my friends. Living in a dormitory was a great experience, because a lot of international students who lives there are also new to the city and are open to make new friends. The dormitory offered a lot of social activities which was a great way to meet new people.

questions.question: Overall, how satisfied were you with the housing available to students? *
Additional comments:
How easy did you find the registration process at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Please describe the registration process at your host institution *
questions.answer: I first checked the course list provided by the University in Bergen for international students. I chose a course in Nordic literary analysis and theory as that is what I am studying at my home university and it sounded very interesting and relevant to my own studies. I took the opportunity to take a course that is not available at my home university, which was a course in ethnomusicology. Then I got a pre-approval for these courses from the exchange department at UCPH. When the semester started I realized that there existed multiple course codes for my Nordic literature course. I decided to switch the course code and got a new pre-approval from UCPH, because the form of examination would be different than what I originally had accepted. By changing the course code I still attended the exact same course but instead of doing both a written and and oral exam, I only had to do a written exam. Because I only attended one semester at UiB it does not affect my future studies. Lastly, because I am Scandinavian it was possible to do the exam in Danish instead of Norwegian even though the course was taught in Norwegian. When I applied for this, my examination code changed to ZNORD-2 which was used on the original course code. This meant that I was an international student who passed a Nordic course in Norwegian. Besides writing in Danish, the examination was exactly the same as for everyone else.

questions.question: What kind of help was available? *
questions.answer: The study guide.

questions.question: How successful were you in registering for the classes you wanted? *
questions.answer: After some time changing course codes, I was very successful.

questions.question: What advice would you offer to future exchange students about registration at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Be sure to get all the information on the courses you can get, and check for deadlines and requirements for the individual courses. Being on exchange in a different university, you have the unique opportunity to try new courses that is not available to you at your home university, so you should consider trying something different and widen your perspectives.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the academic programme at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
Were you a BA or MA student at UCPH when you were on exchange? *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Did you take BA or MA courses at your host university? *
questions.answer: BA

questions.question: Please elaborate on the level of courses *
questions.answer: Because I was a BA student at my home university, I was only able to take BA-leveled courses at UiB.

questions.question: How did the style of teaching at your host institution compare with that of UCPH? *
questions.answer: The style of teaching consisted primarily of lecture based teaching and did not involve the students so much during the courses. This suited my nicely as I am very used to that from my home university and I am very interested in learning from the professors. However, I only had two lectures each week and because the students was not involved as much in the dialogue, it was a bit difficult to socialize with the other students because we did not speak much during the courses and we would only be gathered a few times a month. During the final lectures of my ethnomusicological course each student presented their field work project that we have worked on individually throughout the semester. This was a very nice ending to the semester, as it provided some variation, and it was interesting to learn about the other students' projects.

questions.question: How long were you on exchange? *
questions.answer: 1 semester

questions.question: Please list the courses you were enrolled in during your first semester. *
questions.answer: MUG105 Music in World Cultures and NOLI216 Nordic Literature: Literary Analysis and Theory

questions.question: What specific courses would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: I can recommend both of these courses. If you are interested in music from different cultures than what we are typically being exposed to in the Western world, Music in World Cultures is really interesting. You get to learn about how music is being used differently in other parts of the world and do your own ethnomusicological field work project in Bergen, where you get to explore a music community of your own choice. The Nordic Literature course is very interesting for anyone who deals with Nordic literature and want to be challenged on the topic. You will be exposed to new perspectives, as you will learn about a wide range of theories and why and how to use them.

questions.answer: The books were really expensive.

questions.question: What items were more or less expensive than you expected? *
questions.answer: Fresh vegetables are really expensive and going out to cafés, restaurants, bars etc. is also very expensive.

questions.question: How satisfied were you with the non-academic opportunities (clubs, sports, etc.) at your host institution? *
Additional comments:
What kinds of cultural, athletic and social activities were available for students at your host institution? *
questions.answer: Because I attended a music course, I had music practice spaces available to play either alone or with other people. Besides there was a pool available, various sport courts and the student cultural center Det Akademiske Kvarteret hosted many parties, quizzes and concerts for students. Furthermore, Bergen has a rich associational life and as a student you can become a volunteer in sports teams, photography associations, choirs and environmental associations to name a few.

questions.question: Which non -academic activities would you recommend to future exchange students? Why? *
questions.answer: Go to concerts, quizzes and parties at Hulen and Det Akademiske Kvarteret. They both have student discounts and you can meet Norwegian students where they are a bit more open minded and meet new people in a more casual atmosphere. You should also go on hikes in the mountains as there are plenty of them in the Bergen area, if you are an outdoor person. Most of the museums have student discounts as well and have lots of great exhibitions. Litteraturhuset located in the city center hosts lots of events such as folk music concerts, poetry nights, talks etc. I play music as well, and I went to many jam nights at a bare called Stereo bare on Sundays, which is a great place to socialize and you can also invite your friends to jam with or just hang out.

questions.question: What do you recommend other visiting students see or do on their weekends or holidays? *
questions.answer: Going on hikes as well and see Edvard Griegs house Troldhaugen which is very beautiful. You should also check out the amazing wooden buildings at Bryggen. However, it is a big tourist attraction so be careful not to fall in a tourist trap.

questions.question: How easy was it to adjust to the local culture of your exchange site? *
questions.answer: Denmark and Norway is very similar culturally in a lot of ways, so it was not too difficult. However, nearly every grocery shops, supermarkets and other shops are closed on Sundays and on holidays, so make sure to do your shopping beforehand.

questions.question: Do you have any tips for socializing with local students?
questions.answer: As I mentioned before, you should meet them outside of a university setting. Norwegians as well as Danish people have a reputation of being very reserved so meeting them at concerts, parties or places with a more relaxed atmosphere helps getting the conversation going more easily. Most Norwegians grow up hiking in the mountains and will probably accept an invitation to do so.

questions.question: What, if any, cultural differences did you find particularly challenging? *
questions.answer: Going out to cafés, restaurants, bars and so on is very expensive, so I did not go out as much as I am used to. The fact that almost every shop closes on Sundays and holidays was really irritating at times.

questions.question: What parts of the culture did you most appreciate? *
questions.answer: I come from Denmark so I am primarily used to flat fields everywhere outside of the cities, so having a beautiful view over the mountains everywhere was really amazing.

questions.question: What are the three most important things you would tell a UCPH student who is going to your host institution on exchange? *
questions.answer: Bring hiking boots and gear to go on hiking trips in the mountains. It is a great way to socialize as you make wonderful memories together. The University in Bergen provides a lot of libraries. You will probably spend a lot of time in these, and most of them have a very nice atmosphere, so be sure to check the different ones out, so you know which ones works best for you. If you want to prioritize socializing, you should apply for a living space in a dorm. You will meet a lot of international students there, and if you become friends with them, you live close to each other so it is easy to hang out.

questions.question: Is there any other information that you think might prove useful to future exchange students attending your host institution? *
questions.answer: Remember to check the semester dates, as these were different than what I was used to from my home university. The student guide is very helpful so do not hesitate to ask them anything if you have any questions, and remember to check your e-mail and UiB's digital sources for important information.

questions.question: What was the most rewarding part of your exchange experience? *
questions.answer: Knowing that I am capable of doing well academically in other kinds of courses at a different university than what I am used to, gave me a lot of confidence. Furthermore, it gave me a huge confidence boost knowing that I can do well and thrive both socially and academically in a different country and become good friends with people from different parts of the world.

questions.question: What was the greatest challenge during the exchange? *
questions.answer: To balance being social while also doing my best in the courses. I am a very ambitious student, but a huge part of why I chose to study abroad was to make friends from different countries. Besides that I felt pretty homesick at times, but luckily I had good friends to keep my mind occupied during those periods.

questions.question: Any other comments?
Do you agree to share your travel report with other fellow students? *
questions.answer: Yes
